name: Squalane

lead: Squalane is a stable oil made by hydrogenating squalene, a lipid also found in human skin oil. It is used in serums, facial oils, moisturisers, lip products and hair products to leave skin soft and supple, with a non-greasy feel suited to many skin types.

As an emollient and occlusive lipid it helps the skin hold water, so the smoother, hydrated look appears immediately. Reviews report hydrating and emollient activity mainly from animal and laboratory work, and few controlled trials have tested squalane on its own; one small trial of a fullerene-in-squalane product did not isolate its effect.

paras: It is applied daily as a few drops or a cream, usually as a final step over serums to seal moisture, and also used on lips and hair ends. The feel is immediate, and barrier changes build over weeks.

Sources describe low irritation potential and generally suggest patch testing for sensitive skin. It is sold over the counter as a cosmetic ingredient, and may be plant-derived or historically shark-derived.

angle.text: Squalane is a lightweight oil that seals moisture into skin, so it feels softer and looks smoother and more hydrated right after application. Trial data specific to squalane is limited.

lead: Squalane is a saturated hydrocarbon (C30H62) made by hydrogenating squalene, a lipid found in human sebum, shark liver oil, olives and some other plant sources. It is a colourless, odourless, lightweight oil used mainly as an emollient and skin-conditioning ingredient in moisturisers, serums and hair products.[1][2]

In appearance-focused communities it is discussed as a gentle, non-greasy moisturiser and as a vehicle in skincare products. Published research on squalane itself as a cosmetic active is sparse: most of the literature concerns squalene and squalane as vaccine adjuvant components, as drug-delivery vehicles and as skin-barrier lipids.[2][3] One small randomised trial tested a fullerene-in-squalane cosmetic against wrinkles, but it did not isolate squalane's own effect.[4]

Reviews describe emollient and skin-hydrating activity for squalene and squalane, largely from in vitro and animal work.[2] Squalane is sold over the counter in cosmetic products and appears in some US-listed topical product labels.[5]

Squalane has been used as a cosmetic emollient since the 1950s, and its supply chain has shifted over the past decade from shark liver toward olive-derived and fermentation-derived material, which is why many current products advertise a plant origin.[6]
infobox: Plant-derived (olive, sugarcane) or historically shark liver oil[1][7]
Cosmetic ingredient; sold over the counter

paras: Squalane is the fully hydrogenated form of squalene, a branched 30-carbon triterpene hydrocarbon. Removing squalene's double bonds makes the molecule more resistant to oxidation, which is the main reason the saturated form is used in finished cosmetics.[1] Human sebum naturally contains squalene (roughly 13 percent in one review), while squalane itself is a manufactured or isolated derivative.[2]

Historically squalane was obtained from deep-sea shark liver oil. Reviews on squalene supply note ecological concerns about shark harvesting and describe plant-derived and fermentation-based sources as alternatives; current cosmetic squalane is commonly marketed as olive- or sugarcane-derived.[1][7][8]

Squalane is used as an emollient in moisturisers, facial oils, serums, lip and hair products. Product descriptions and secondary sources characterise it as lightweight, quickly absorbed and suitable for oily or acne-prone skin, although these properties are asserted mainly in cosmetic-industry and general-reference descriptions rather than in controlled trials of squalane alone.[1][2]

A topical product label listing squalane with niacinamide in a dark-spot corrector advises external use only, avoiding the eyes, discontinuing if irritation occurs and using sunscreen during the day.[5]

Squalane and squalene emulsions are used as oil components of vaccine adjuvants and as drug-delivery vehicles; this is a separate, well-documented use unrelated to appearance.[3][9][10] Squalane-containing adjuvants were also tested in an early malaria sporozoite vaccine trial.[11]

Stratum corneum lipids are an important determinant of the skin's water-holding function, and experiments replenishing sebum-derived lipids on lipid-depleted human skin found recovery of water-holding properties.[12][13] Squalane is an occlusive, lipid-like hydrocarbon, and reviews credit squalene and squalane with hydrating and emollient effects in animal and in vitro models.[2] An ex vivo study of squalane-based emulsions examined their influence on skin penetration of polyphenols.[14]

Squalane and squalene have been the subject of a safety review in the International Journal of Toxicology (2023).[15] General-reference descriptions report low irritation potential at cosmetic concentrations and recommend patch testing for sensitive individuals.[1] No notable adverse-event literature specific to topical squalane is available in the reviewed sources.

The hydrogenation of squalene to give squalane was first reported in 1916, and squalane entered cosmetics as an emollient in the 1950s.[6] Its appeal to formulators was practical: because the molecule is fully saturated it does not undergo auto-oxidation, so it stays stable on the shelf and does not turn rancid the way squalene can, and it costs less to work with.[6]

For decades the raw material was squalene taken from shark livers; a Wikipedia summary puts the figure at roughly 3,000 sharks to produce a ton of squalane.[6] Environmental concerns led manufacturers to commercialise olive, rice and sugarcane routes, and by 2014 these were reported to supply about 40 percent of the industry total.[6]

Two plant-based routes are in commercial use. In olive squalane, squalene is extracted from olive-oil processing residues and then hydrogenated. In sugarcane squalane, sugars are fermented by a genetically modified yeast to make farnesene, which is dimerised to isosqualene and then hydrogenated.[6] Reviews on squalene supply also describe synthetic-biology and yeast production as ways to reduce reliance on shark harvesting.[3][7]

Product pages and ingredient discussions therefore tend to label squalane by origin (olive, sugarcane, or unspecified). The molecule produced is chemically the same compound whichever route is used, according to the general references.[1][6]

In the European Union the ingredient is declared on cosmetic labels under the standardised INCI name Squalane, and the European Commission's CosIng inventory lists skin-conditioning and emollient functions for it.[6] The general reference literature describes squalane as having low acute toxicity and not being a significant skin irritant or sensitiser.[6] The 2023 International Journal of Toxicology review of squalane and squalene is the most recent formal safety assessment of the ingredient.[15]

Squalane appears in basic moisturisers, face oils and single-ingredient bottles, and it is often positioned as a way to add softness and a smoother skin surface without a heavy feel. Skincare writers commonly describe layering it after water-based serums so that it seals in moisture, although these routines come from product guidance and general practice rather than controlled studies of squalane.[1]

The skin-barrier research that is usually cited alongside it shows that replenishing sebum-type lipids on lipid-depleted skin restored water-holding capacity, which is the physiological reasoning behind using lipid-like emollients to reduce a dry, scaly look.[12][13] People who use it for hair apply it as a light oil for shine and softness, as described in general references.[1]

The two names are easy to confuse. Squalene, the unsaturated parent molecule, was first isolated in 1906 by the Japanese chemist Mitsumaru Tsujimoto from the oil of deep-sea shark liver, and its structure was confirmed by laboratory synthesis in 1931.[16] Roughly 12 percent of the squalene in the human body is found in sebum, the skin's own oil, which is one reason the molecule is described as skin-identical.[16][2] Squalane is the hydrogenated, shelf-stable counterpart that formulators generally choose for finished products because it does not oxidise as readily as squalene.[1]

Shark liver oil from deep-water species is the most concentrated natural source of squalene, at roughly half or more of the oil by weight, while plant oils such as amaranth and olive contain far smaller percentages. Engineered microbes have also been used to make it.[16] These production routes explain why labels increasingly name an olive, sugarcane or fermentation origin.[16][8]

sections.h: Safety record in cosmetics and vaccines
paras: Toxicology summaries cited in general references report low acute toxicity at cosmetic concentrations and describe squalene as not being a significant contact irritant or allergen.[16][15] The 2023 International Journal of Toxicology review of squalane and squalene is the formal cosmetic-ingredient safety assessment for the pair.[15]

Squalene-based emulsions are also used in some adjuvanted influenza vaccines, a separate pharmaceutical use. The World Health Organization has stated that squalene occurs naturally in the body and that adjuvanted vaccines containing it have been given to many millions of people in Europe without significant vaccine-related adverse events, according to the Wikipedia summary of its position.[16] Claims linking squalene to Gulf War illness have been examined and rejected by health authorities, and squalene was not an ingredient in the vaccines concerned.[16]

sections.h: Where it appears in an appearance routine
paras: In skincare, squalane typically appears as one ingredient among several rather than as the headline active. Product descriptions list it in moisturisers, facial oils, lip balms, makeup removers and hair-smoothing products, where its role is to soften the skin surface and reduce water loss.[1] Because it is lightweight, people who dislike heavy creams sometimes use a few drops under or over other products; manufacturers market it as suitable for oily and acne-prone skin, a claim that rests on product descriptions and ingredient references rather than comparative trials.[1][2]

Combination products are common. The listed niacinamide dark-spot corrector label, for example, pairs squalane with a pigment-targeting active and carries standard cosmetic directions such as daytime sunscreen use.[5] In these formulations squalane acts as the emollient base that makes the product spreadable and less drying.

Controlled human studies of squalane as a standalone cosmetic active are scarce. A randomised controlled trial reported in 2010 evaluated fullerene-C60 dissolved in squalane as an anti-wrinkle cosmetic; because the active comparison was the fullerene preparation, it does not establish an effect of squalane alone.[4] Other human work involves squalane as an adjuvant component in vaccines rather than as a skin product.[11]
